title: Stress, Burnout & Psychological Demands
description: First unit: A busy week versus chronic overload. Work through real situations, competing explanations and practical choices.

modules.title: A busy week versus chronic overload

lessons.title: What is really happening?
lessons.teach: Priya runs a busy support service. Sam is a colleague who has noticed Priya working late for weeks.

nodes.title: Watch the conversation
nodes.prompt: Listen closely to what each person says and what still remains uncertain.
nodes.explanation: Persistent demands exceed Priya's available time and influence. Recovery becomes difficult because the conditions that created the overload remain in place.
nodes.counterexample: Burnout is an occupational phenomenon, not a diagnosis established by tiredness alone. Individual coping cannot compensate indefinitely for unmanageable demands.
nodes.sources: WHO ICD-11 occupational burnout; Bakker & Demerouti (2007), Job Demands–Resources model.
nodes.scenario: Priya runs a busy support service. Sam is a colleague who has noticed Priya working late for weeks.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I used to recover after a busy week. Lately I wake up tired before work even starts.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: We've had an unusually demanding month. Is there any sign the workload is easing?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: They added another caseload yesterday, and the vacant post still hasn't been filled.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Have you had any say in how much you're expected to manage?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I asked what could be postponed. My manager said everything was a priority.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: What happens when you take your scheduled breaks?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: The backlog grows and I get messages asking when reports will be ready.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: So rest is being treated as time you have to make up, rather than part of the job?

options.label: The behaviour may serve the proposed function in this case. We would need broader evidence before treating it as a stable characteristic.
options.feedback: This retains a useful process explanation without generalising beyond the evidence.

options.label: The person has not confirmed their own motive, so we should avoid making any psychological inference at all.
options.feedback: Direct self-report helps, but a tentative formulation can still be tested against observed circumstances.

options.label: The response fits the theory, so it is likely to occur in most situations that threaten the person.
options.feedback: Generalising to different settings requires repeated observations, not theoretical resemblance alone.

nodes.title: Which evidence matters most?
nodes.prompt: You want to distinguish the working hypothesis from its strongest alternative. Which investigation would provide the most discriminating information?
nodes.explanation: Investigate a difference that the rival explanations predict. Compare demands, control and resources over time, including what happens when tasks are formally reprioritised.
nodes.counterexample: Burnout is an occupational phenomenon, not a diagnosis established by tiredness alone. Individual coping cannot compensate indefinitely for unmanageable demands.
nodes.sources: WHO ICD-11 occupational burnout; Bakker & Demerouti (2007), Job Demands–Resources model.

options.feedback: The strength of a feeling matters, but it does not establish its cause.

options.label: Compare demands, control and resources over time, including what happens when tasks are formally reprioritised.
options.feedback: This gathers information that could strengthen or weaken the explanation, rather than merely confirming an impression.

options.label: Ask the person affected whether the behaviour seems consistent with their overall impression of the speaker.
options.feedback: Impact and perception matter for responding; they are less decisive about the other person’s hidden motives.

options.label: Find one more occasion when the characters disagreed, without checking what the circumstances were.
options.feedback: Another incident is useful only if we compare the circumstances and plausible explanations.

lessons.title: Try it in another situation
lessons.teach: Apply the way of reasoning to a different situation. Do not import the first case’s verdict.

nodes.title: A new situation
nodes.body:
A nurse takes repeated wellbeing workshops while staffing shortages and unsafe workload expectations remain unchanged.

Decide what you can infer from this example without assuming the same explanation must apply.
nodes.sources: WHO ICD-11 occupational burnout; Bakker & Demerouti (2007), Job Demands–Resources model.

nodes.title: Apply the method elsewhere
nodes.prompt: Consider this different situation: A nurse takes repeated wellbeing workshops while staffing shortages and unsafe workload expectations remain unchanged. What is the strongest next step?
nodes.explanation: Transfer the reasoning method rather than an explanation from the first case. Burnout is an occupational phenomenon, not a diagnosis established by tiredness alone. Individual coping cannot compensate indefinitely for unmanageable demands.

options.label: Treat the visible similarity as a reliable indication that the behaviour has the same psychological function.
options.feedback: Similar behaviours can protect very different interests depending on the context.

options.label: Consider what the person could be trying to gain or avoid, then test that explanation against the circumstances and credible alternatives.
options.feedback: This asks what the behaviour might accomplish and how we could check.

options.label: Postpone all interpretation until the person can give an account of their private motives.
options.feedback: A perfect self-report may be unavailable. Tentative, revisable inferences can still be useful.

options.label: Judge whether the behaviour is socially acceptable first, since that provides the best evidence about why it happened.
options.feedback: Judging the consequences of a behaviour is important, but consequences do not by themselves establish motive.

nodes.title: Fact or inference?
nodes.prompt: Sort the exact words spoken from explanations about what those words might mean.
nodes.explanation: The words are evidence. Both the preferred explanation and its rival are interpretations requiring further testing. Burnout is an occupational phenomenon, not a diagnosis established by tiredness alone. Individual coping cannot compensate indefinitely for unmanageable demands.

nodes.title: An idea worth carrying forward
nodes.body:
Persistent demands exceed Priya's available time and influence. Recovery becomes difficult because the conditions that created the overload remain in place.

Burnout is an occupational phenomenon, not a diagnosis established by tiredness alone. Individual coping cannot compensate indefinitely for unmanageable demands.

The purpose of the exercise is to make a better-supported judgement and choose a proportionate next step.
nodes.sources: WHO ICD-11 occupational burnout; Bakker & Demerouti (2007), Job Demands–Resources model.
